15.1|Which foundational research project marked the official beginning of the Hawthorne Studies at Western Electric's plant between 1924 and 1927?|The illumination experiments testing the relationship between lighting intensity and worker productivity|The relay assembly room experiments focusing on rest periods and supervision style|The bank wiring observation room study examining informal group productivity restrictions|The mass employee interview program mapping out employee grievances and workplace attitudes|Option A|The illumination experiments were the first phase of the Hawthorne Studies designed to test whether lighting levels impacted worker output.
15.1|What primary behavioral phenomenon was discovered during the relay assembly room phase of the Hawthorne Studies?|The Hawthorne Effect where workers increase their productivity simply because they receive special attention and observation|The Peter Principle where employees rise to the level of their respective incompetence within a hierarchy|Groupthink where cohesive teams suppress dissenting views to achieve unanimous organizational consensus|Parkinson Law stating that work expands to fill the time available for its completion|Option B|The Hawthorne Effect explains that workers improve their performance when they realize they are being observed and valued.
15.1|How did Elton Mayo and his research team conceptually redefine the typical worker following the Hawthorne findings?|As an economic man driven strictly by financial incentives and piece-rate maximization|As a social man motivated primarily by group belonging recognition and interpersonal dynamics|As a self-actualized individual driven by intrinsic motivation and creative task autonomy|As a rational actor seeking to maximize organizational utility through formal bureaucratic rules|Option C|The Human Relations Theory established that workers respond deeply to social needs rather than purely monetary motives.
15.1|What key workplace dynamic was uncovered during the bank wiring observation room study?|The presence of informal group norms that penalized both rate busters and chiselers to maintain group harmony|The direct correlation between higher managerial supervision and strict adherence to formal output quotas|The absolute dominance of monetary incentives over all other forms of informal workplace communication|The complete eradication of unofficial workplace cliques under democratic leadership styles|Option D|The bank wiring room study highlighted how informal groups enforce internal norms regarding acceptable output limits.

2.1|Which of the following best defines the integral view of public administration as advanced by L.D. White and Dimock?|It focuses exclusively on top managerial functions such as planning and directing|It encompasses all activities undertaken from top management to manual labor to accomplish goals|It limits administrative scope strictly to legislative policymaking|It views administration solely as a clerical function within the private sector|Option B|The integral view argues that public administration includes the sum total of all activities—managerial, technical, clerical, and manual—undertaken to achieve an objective.

3.1|Which characteristic primarily defines Public Administration when viewed as an art?|Empirical observation of structural hierarchies|Systematic testing of verifiable organizational principles|Personal skill and intuition applied in volatile social situations|Universal laws governing bureaucratic efficiency|Option C|Viewing public administration as an art emphasizes personal skill, intuition, and practical experience rather than rigid mechanical rules.

3.1|What was a major argument raised by Robert Dahl regarding the scientific status of public administration?|It lacks mathematical formulas for budgeting|It cannot be a pure science because of normative values and unpredictable human behavior|It relies too heavily on historical archives rather than current data|It operates identically across all sovereign democratic nations|Option C|Robert Dahl argued that public administration cannot be a pure science due to the influence of normative values, unpredictable human behavior, and cultural relativity.

3.1|Why does unpredictable human behavior complicate public administration's claim to being a pure science?|It prevents employees from ever receiving promotions or pay increases|It makes controlled laboratory experimentation and absolute predictability nearly impossible|It forces organizations to abandon all forms of formal institutional structure|It ensures that all administrative decisions are made entirely by computers|Option B|Unlike natural sciences that study constant physical laws, public administration deals with human behavior which is inherently variable and difficult to predict.
3.1|What role do normative values play in public administration according to the critique of it as a science?|They provide exact numerical metrics for measuring bureaucratic output|They introduce subjective ideas of what ought to be rather than purely objective facts|They ensure that administrative systems operate without any human intervention|They completely eliminate the need for leadership in volatile situations|Option C|Normative values involve subjective judgments about goals and ethics, which complicate the pursuit of value-free pure science in administration.

14.1|What is the primary purpose of the Scalar Chain principle alongside its exception mechanism known as the Gangplank?|To ensure that all disciplinary actions are recorded and reported directly to the board of directors|To maintain the formal line of authority while permitting horizontal communication between peers in urgent cases to speed up work|To decentralize decision-making authority completely down to frontline operational workers|To eliminate all vertical hierarchies and establish a completely flattened democratic organization|Option B|The scalar chain outlines the line of authority from top to bottom, while the gangplank allows lateral communication between peers when going through the formal chain would cause harmful delay.
14.1|How does Fayol distinguish Unity of Direction from Unity of Command?|Unity of direction applies exclusively to financial matters while unity of command applies to personnel|Unity of direction focuses on a single plan and head for activities sharing the same objective whereas unity of command ensures an employee takes orders from only one boss|Unity of direction refers to horizontal peer coordination while unity of command refers to vertical upward feedback|Unity of direction requires centralizing all power while unity of command requires decentralizing authority|Option B|Unity of direction ensures all related organizational activities are grouped under one plan and guided by a single leader, whereas unity of command concerns receiving orders from a single supervisor.
14.1|Which principle of management emphasizes that the overall goals of the organization must take precedence over the personal agendas of individual employees?|Centralization|Equity|Subordination of individual interest to the general interest|Esprit de Corps|Option C|This principle dictates that the interest of one employee or a group should not prevail over the interests of the organization as a whole.
14.1|Which concept within Fayol's framework refers to harmony and strong team spirit building unity and morale among organizational members?|Esprit de Corps|Initiative|Stability of tenure of personnel|Discipline|Option A|Esprit de Corps promotes team spirit, harmony, and a sense of unity among personnel, which Fayol considered vital for organizational strength.
14.1|What does Fayol's principle of Equity imply for managers within an administrative structure?|Managers must treat all employees with a combination of kindliness and justice to encourage loyalty and devotion|Managers must ensure that all workers receive identical rates of pay regardless of their specific duties|Managers must distribute ownership shares equally among all operational staff members|Managers must rotate every worker through different departments annually to maintain fairness|Option A|Equity combines kindliness and justice on the part of managers toward their subordinates to inspire loyalty and a fair working environment.
14.1|Why did Henri Fayol advocate for the Stability of tenure of personnel principle in top-management administration?|Because frequent turnover of management staff is inefficient and hinders organizational learning and stability|Because permanent employment contracts eliminate the need for any formal employee performance evaluations|Because workers who stay in one position for life automatically achieve peak physical productivity|Because changing jobs frequently violates the strict command structure of the scalar chain|Option A|Fayol stressed that time is required for an employee to get used to work and succeed in it well, making excessive staff turnover inefficient.

15.1|What core assumption about worker motivation did Elton Mayo's Human Relations Theory challenge?|Workers are primarily motivated by social belonging and group recognition|Workers respond favorably to attention and observational care|Workers are rational economic actors driven chiefly by financial compensation|Workers form informal structures that regulate daily output norms|Option C|Classical theory assumed workers were primarily economic men driven by money, whereas the Hawthorne studies proved social factors and recognition hold greater motivational weight.
15.1|What phenomenon was primarily observed during the Illumination Experiments at the Hawthorne Works?|Worker productivity increased regardless of whether lighting levels were raised or lowered|Production dropped drastically whenever supervisory oversight was removed|Workers formed strict quotas to punish high-performing rate busters|Employees demanded higher hourly wages after individual interviews were conducted|Option A|The illumination experiments showed that output fluctuated or rose due to attention and psychological factors rather than physical illumination changes alone.
15.1|How does the Hawthorne Effect manifest in an organizational setting?|Employees deliberately reduce their output to protest against management policies|Workers temporarily improve their performance simply because they are being observed and given attention|Management relies solely on financial bonuses to curb absenteeism|Informal groups enforce strict codes of conduct against non-conformists|Option B|The Hawthorne Effect describes how individuals modify their behavior—typically improving productivity—in response to their awareness of being studied or given special attention.
15.1|What was a primary finding derived from the Mass Interviews phase of the Hawthorne Studies?|Workers wanted stricter regulations and fewer breaks during shifts|Employee morale and attitudes were deeply shaped by personal backgrounds and workplace social contexts|Financial incentives were proven to be the sole determinant of job satisfaction|Formal organizational charts completely dictate daily interpersonal interactions|Option B|Mass interviews revealed that workers' complaints and satisfaction were tied to complex social dynamics, personal histories, and overall workplace environments rather than just physical working conditions.
15.1|In the context of the Bank Wiring Room phase, what role did informal group norms play among workers?|They enforced natural output ceilings to protect slower workers from management pressure|They encouraged maximum individual competition through piece-rate bonuses|They ensured complete compliance with formal administrative rules and procedures|They eliminated all forms of interpersonal conflict within the department|Option A|The bank wiring room demonstrated that informal groups establish internal norms and restrictions, branding high producers as rate busters and low producers as chiselers to maintain group equilibrium.
15.1|How did Elton Mayo and his researchers characterize the typical employee based on the Hawthorne findings?|As a solitary economic actor driven entirely by cost-benefit calculations|As a social man whose behavior is largely dictated by group dynamics and belonging|As an administrative machine programmed to follow standard operating procedures|As an isolated individual impervious to peer influence and supervisory recognition|Option B|The core principle derived from the studies is that workers are social men motivated by belonging, recognition, and group dynamics rather than mere financial incentives.
15.1|What specific term did the Hawthorne researchers use to describe workers who exceeded the informal group output restrictions?|Chiselers|Rate busters|Free riders|Social loafers|Option B|Workers who produced too much and violated the informal group norms were labeled rate busters, while those who produced too little were called chiselers.
15.1|What was the primary focus of the Relay Assembly Room experiment within the broader Hawthorne investigations?|Testing the impact of varied rest periods and work hours on output and morale|Measuring the precise chemical toxicity of paint in manufacturing plants|Evaluating the effectiveness of automated machinery versus manual labor|Assessing the financial impact of profit-sharing schemes on individual productivity|Option A|The relay assembly room study manipulated variables like rest pauses, work hours, and food provisions to observe their direct effects on worker output and satisfaction.
15.1|Which major theoretical critique emerged as a direct legacy of the Human Relations Theory developed from the Hawthorne Studies?|It completely ignored the existence of informal groups within formal organizations|It overemphasized psychological and social harmony while underestimating structural conflict and power dynamics|It relied exclusively on mathematical modeling to predict employee behavior|It championed the view that financial incentives are the only reliable motivational tool|Option B|A common critique of the human relations school is that it romanticized workplace harmony and neglected structural, political, and economic conflicts inherent in organizations.

13.1|Which specific technique was utilized by Scientific Management to discover the single best way to execute a physical task?|Participative action research|Time-and-motion studies|Financial auditing and budget variance analysis|Psychological stress testing|Option B|Time-and-motion studies were the primary empirical tools used to break down tasks into component movements, eliminate waste, and find the one best way.
13.1|What was the purpose of the mental revolution advocated under Taylor's principles?|To shift the focus of management and labor from fighting over surplus distribution to cooperating on increasing total output|To eliminate hierarchical structures entirely and establish worker-owned cooperatives|To replace physical labor with automated robotics across all manufacturing sectors|To merge public administration agencies with private sector corporate boards|Option A|The mental revolution required both management and workers to stop quarreling over profit division and instead unite their efforts to maximize organizational productivity.
13.1|How did the scientific management approach fundamentally alter the selection and development of personnel?|By relying exclusively on seniority and personal recommendations from existing workers|By introducing systematic scientific selection and specialized training for employees|By allowing workers to freely choose any task based on their daily preferences|By outsourcing hiring decisions to external community employment agencies|Option B|Scientific management discarded haphazard hiring in favor of scientifically matching individuals to jobs suited to their abilities and providing targeted training.
13.1|What mechanism was central to Taylor's theory for incentivizing higher employee productivity and output?|A guaranteed annual salary regardless of output volume|A piece-rate wage system tied directly to units produced|Seniority-based automatic annual pay increments|Profit-sharing dividends distributed equally among all departments|Option B|The piece-rate wage system rewarded workers financially based on their specific output volume, encouraging them to exceed standard production quotas.
13.1|What was the structural purpose of functional foremanship in Taylor's framework?|To centralize all supervisory authority into a single supreme general manager|To divide shop floor supervision into multiple specialized functional experts guiding workers|To rotate managerial positions weekly among rank-and-file workers|To separate administrative policy formulation entirely from operational execution|Option B|Functional foremanship replaced the single traditional boss with multiple specialized supervisors, each focusing on a distinct aspect of production or training.
13.1|What was a primary criticism leveled against F.W. Taylor's Scientific Management Theory?|It treated human workers as mere machine parts and overemphasized them as economic men|It was excessively democratic and slowed down decision-making processes to a crawl|It ignored the importance of technical efficiency and production speed entirely|It relied too heavily on spiritual and psychological motivation rather than financial rewards|Option A|Critics frequently condemned Scientific Management for reducing human employees to mechanical extensions of machinery driven solely by economic incentives.
13.1|In Taylor's framework, how was the division of responsibility structured between management and workers?|Management assumed responsibility for planning and scientific design, while workers focused on execution|Management handled daily manual tasks, while workers planned organizational strategy|Both groups shared identical operational duties without any functional specialization|Workers assumed total control over operational planning while management handled sales|Option A|Taylor advocated for a clear division where managers used scientific principles to plan and prepare work, leaving workers responsible for executing those specific instructions.

14.1|How does Fayol distinguish between Unity of Command and Unity of Direction?|Unity of direction focuses on a single head and plan for activities sharing the same objective, while unity of command focuses on receiving orders from one boss.|Unity of command deals with departmental budgets while unity of direction deals with employee discipline.|Unity of direction requires a strict scalar chain whereas unity of command permits lateral gangplank communication.|Unity of command is a top management function while unity of direction is exclusively a lower-level operational practice.|Option A|Unity of direction ensures all related activities have one plan and one leader, whereas unity of command ensures each worker answers to only one supervisor.
14.1|What does Fayol's principle of the Gangplank (Scalar Chain) primarily facilitate within an organization?|Strict adherence to hierarchical reporting channels for all decisions|Rapid lateral communication between peers at the same organizational level without going through upper management chains|Immediate dismissal of insubordinate workers without due process|Centralization of all financial resources at the executive level|Option B|The gangplank allows direct lateral communication between employees at similar levels to speed up work, provided their superiors are informed.

15.1|What phenomenon was primarily observed during the Relay Assembly Room experiments at the Hawthorne Works?|Physical fatigue caused a sharp decline in overall daily production rates|The introduction of bright lighting completely paralyzed the workers output capacity|Worker productivity increased due to special attention and observation rather than physical changes|Financial bonuses caused intense competition and hostility among assembly operators|Option C|The Hawthorne Effect demonstrates that employees boost their output when they feel singled out and given special attention.

11.1|What significant financial innovation did the 1976 Local Government Reform secure for local authorities?|Direct statutory revenue allocation from the national pool|Total reliance on international donor grants and foreign aid|Exclusive authority to collect personal income tax nationwide|The power to print local municipal currency notes|Option A|The reform guaranteed financial viability by introducing direct statutory revenue allocation to local councils from the federation account.
11.1|Which of the following constitutes a primary internal source of Internally Generated Revenue (IGR) for local governments?|Customs tariffs and international cargo duties|Tenement rates and local market levies collected within the district|Corporate profits tax levied on multinational conglomerates|Value-added tax generated from nationwide digital transactions|Option B|Tenement rates and market levies represent core internal revenue sources that local governments directly collect from their jurisdictions.
11.1|Why is a single-tier uniform structure considered advantageous for local government administration under the 1976 model?|It eliminates structural confusion and standardizes service delivery functions|It completely prevents the state government from exercising oversight|It concentrates all national legislative powers at the grassroots level|It removes the need for any form of local revenue generation|Option C|A uniform single-tier structure clarifies administrative jurisdictions and standardizes the scope of service delivery responsibilities across different councils.
11.1|In the context of multi-level governance, what makes local government uniquely suited for grassroots service delivery?|Its physical proximity and responsiveness to the immediate needs of local inhabitants|Its capacity to mobilize heavy military defense assets rapidly|Its ability to negotiate bilateral treaties with foreign municipal bodies|Its control over central bank interest rate adjustments|Option A|Proximity to the populace allows local governments to understand and respond more effectively to grassroots community needs than distant central agencies.
11.1|Apart from federation account allocations, what is another official external source of revenue for local governments?|State government allocations and joint account distributions|Direct grants from foreign sovereign wealth funds|Revenue generated from national railway ticket sales|Proceeds from federal maritime shipping licenses|Option A|Local governments receive financial support not only from the federation account but also through designated allocations and statutory distributions from state governments.
11.1|What fundamental governance objective is achieved by integrating local government into the formal statutory structure?|Enhancing democratic participation and accountability at the community level|Centralizing all bureaucratic decision-making in the federal capital|Eliminating the need for citizen feedback mechanisms entirely|Transferring all judicial powers from courts to municipal councils|Option A|Statutory integration empowers citizens to participate directly in governance, thereby strengthening accountability and local democracy.
11.1|How does the collection of tenement rates contribute to the fiscal health of a local government?|It provides a predictable and recurring stream of internally generated revenue from property owners|It eliminates the need for any federal or state financial transfers|It serves as a penalty tax to discourage real estate development|It functions as an external loan repaid by the federal treasury|Option C|Tenement rates act as a reliable source of internally generated revenue, reducing total fiscal dependency on higher tiers of government.

13.1|What phenomenon did F.W. Taylor primarily seek to eliminate through his scientific approach?|Worker soldiering|Bureaucratic red tape|Functional decentralization|Routine administrative friction|Option A|Taylor designed scientific management explicitly to eliminate worker soldiering, which is the deliberate restriction of output by employees.
13.1|What did Scientific Management seek to replace traditional methods with?|Political patronage|Rule-of-thumb|Intuitive leadership|Charismatic authority|Option B|Taylor argued that traditional rule-of-thumb methods should be replaced by systematic, scientifically tested workplace practices.
13.1|Which mechanism was heavily utilized to determine the 'one best way' to perform a task?|Time-and-motion studies|Participatory action research|Case study observation|Historical comparative analysis|Option A|Time-and-motion studies measure worker movements and time requirements to establish standardized, optimal work procedures.
13.1|What core principle involves matching workers' physical and mental abilities to specific tasks?|Mental revolution cooperation|Functional foremanship|Scientific selection and training|Division of responsibility|Option C|Scientific selection and training ensures employees are placed in roles that align best with their inherent capabilities.
13.1|What did Taylor mean by the term mental revolution?|A psychological breakdown caused by assembly line stress|A complete shift in mindset toward mutual cooperation between management and workers|A transition from manual labor to administrative cognitive tasks|An ideological revolt against industrial capitalism|Option B|The mental revolution requires both management and workers to focus on increasing surplus rather than fighting over how to divide it.
13.1|How did Taylor propose to divide duties between management and the workforce?|Management plans and sets standards while workers execute the physical labor|Workers decide production methods while managers handle finances|Management performs all labor while workers act as supervisors|Both groups share identical operational and planning responsibilities equally|Option A|The division of responsibility shifts planning and intellectual work to management while workers focus strictly on execution.
13.1|Which compensation structure is most closely associated with F.W. Taylor's efficiency models?|Piece-rate wage system|Profit-sharing dividends|Fixed annual salary with bonuses|Seniority-based incremental pay|Option A|The piece-rate wage system incentivizes higher productivity by paying workers strictly based on the number of units they produce.
13.1|What organizational structure did Taylor advocate to replace the traditional single-supervisor model?|Functional foremanship|Matrix organizational design|Divisional product structures|Flattened horizontal hierarchies|Option A|Functional foremanship replaces a single boss with multiple specialized supervisors, each overseeing a specific aspect of the work.
13.1|What was a primary criticism leveled against F.W. Taylor's Scientific Management Theory?|It treated human workers merely as interchangeable machine parts (economic man)|It ignored economic incentives entirely in favor of social rewards|It promoted excessive decentralization and employee autonomy|It relied too heavily on psychological counseling and emotional intelligence|Option A|Critics argued that viewing workers as economic men who respond only to financial incentives reduces them to machine parts.
15.1|Which major historical research project served as the foundation for the Human Relations Theory in public administration?|The Hawthorne Studies|The Pendleton Act Investigations|The Brownlow Committee Inquiries|The Weberian Bureaucracy Audits|Option A|The Hawthorne Studies conducted between 1924 and 1932 at Western Electric Company shifted focus from mechanical efficiency to human relations.
15.1|What core concept did Elton Mayo and his associates introduce regarding the nature of workers?|Workers are primarily Economic Men driven exclusively by monetary rewards|Workers are Social Men motivated by belonging recognition and group dynamics|Workers are Rational Automata driven entirely by formal rules and hierarchy|Workers are Isolated Individuals unaffected by peer pressure or leadership style|Option B|The Human Relations Theory established that workers respond primarily to social needs group dynamics and recognition rather than just economic incentives.
15.1|What was the primary finding of the illumination experiments in the Hawthorne Studies?|Changing lighting levels directly and predictably altered worker productivity regardless of social factors|Illumination had no impact because workers worked slower in brighter environments|Worker output changed due to the psychological attention of being observed rather than the physical lighting adjustments|Financial incentives completely overshadowed any physical changes made to the workspace illumination|Option C|The illumination experiments revealed that productivity fluctuated due to the attention researchers paid to the workers, marking an early observation of the Hawthorne Effect.
15.1|What phenomenon does the Hawthorne Effect specifically describe in organizational settings?|A permanent decrease in output caused by strict enforcement of formal administrative rules|An increase in worker performance and morale resulting from the special attention of being studied|The natural tendency of workers to form secret unions against oppressive management practices|The absolute reliance of employees on high hourly wages to maintain sustained motivation|Option B|The Hawthorne Effect occurs when individuals modify their behavior or improve performance simply because they know they are being observed or given special attention.
15.1|Which specific phase of the Hawthorne Studies revealed the powerful influence of informal group norms and peer pressure?|The Illumination Experiments|The Relay Assembly Test Room|The Mass Interview Programme|The Bank Wiring Observation Room|Option D|The Bank Wiring Observation Room highlighted how informal groups establish their own internal norms restricting output to control workplace pace.
15.1|In the context of the Bank Wiring Room findings what term was used to describe workers who produced more than the informal group quota?|Rate busters|Chiselers|Free riders|Social loafers|Option A|Group norms in the Bank Wiring Room labeled high producers as rate busters and those who produced too little as chiselers to protect group equilibrium.
15.1|What was a primary objective of the mass interview programme conducted during the Hawthorne Studies?|To evaluate the technical skill levels of assembly line workers for potential promotions|To allow workers to express their grievances and understand how personal and social factors affect morale|To determine the exact financial bonus structure required to maximize daily manufacturing output|To test whether physical fatigue caused a decline in late-shift productivity|Option B|Mass interviews were designed to let workers voice their feelings about supervision and working conditions uncovering the importance of social sentiments.
15.1|How did the Human Relations Theory fundamentally challenge classical management theories like those of Taylor and Weber?|By arguing that organizations should abandon all hierarchies and adopt total anarchy|By proving that financial compensation is completely irrelevant to worker productivity|By shifting the primary administrative focus from formal structures and economic efficiency to human and social factors|By demonstrating that workers perform best when completely isolated from one another|Option C|Classical theories viewed workers as mechanical economic cogs whereas Human Relations Theory emphasized psychological social and informal group dimensions.
15.1|What informal group behavior was observed regarding workers who produced significantly below the established group norm?|They were celebrated as innovators of efficient work methods|They were labeled as chiselers and subjected to informal social pressure|They were immediately promoted to supervisory management positions|They were granted extra financial incentives by the company administration|Option B|Workers who produced too little were called chiselers by their peers who applied social pressure to bring their output in line with group expectations.
15.1|What overarching conclusion did the Hawthorne Studies provide regarding organizational productivity?|Productivity is exclusively governed by the physical design of tools and machinery|Administrative rules are the sole determinant of employee satisfaction and performance|Social interactions group dynamics and psychological recognition significantly shape worker output|Formal organizational charts dictate all actual workplace behavior and communication flows|Option C|The overarching takeaway of the Hawthorne Studies is that social relationships group norms and recognition play a critical role in determining productivity.

3.1|What was a primary argument raised by Robert Dahl in his critique of public administration as a science?|Administrative principles are universally applicable across all distinct cultures|Human behavior is completely predictable under controlled laboratory settings|Administrative science cannot be pure due to the influence of normative values and cultural relativity|Public administration relies exclusively on physical science laws rather than social frameworks|Option C|Robert Dahl argued that public administration cannot be a pure science because administrative principles are culturally relative and bound by normative values.
3.1|According to Robert Dahl why does unpredictable human behavior challenge public administration as a science?|People always act in exact accordance with established administrative rules|Human actions are erratic and cannot be easily standardized into absolute scientific laws|Citizens refuse to interact with government agencies during crises|Employees in public organizations never experience personal biases|Option B|Unpredictable human behavior introduces variables that prevent public administration from achieving the absolute predictability found in physical sciences.
3.1|How does the concept of cultural relativity affect administrative principles according to Robert Dahl?|Principles that work in one national culture may fail or require heavy modification in another|Culture has zero impact on how organizations operate globally|All administrative structures are identical regardless of geographic location|Cultural norms completely eliminate the need for organizational hierarchies|Option A|Cultural relativity means that administrative principles cannot be universally applied because they change based on cultural contexts.
3.1|Which aspect of public administration is best demonstrated by a leader navigating an unprecedented social crisis using judgment and tact?|The scientific methodology of administration|The artistic and practical side of public administration|The mechanical application of structural hierarchy|The mathematical measurement of span of control|Option B|Navigating volatile social situations requires the personal skill and practical experience characteristic of administration as an art.
3.1|Why did Robert Dahl state that public administration is heavily influenced by normative values?|Administrative decisions often involve judgments about what ought to be rather than just objective facts|Public administrators are legally forbidden from holding personal opinions|Normative values can be completely eliminated through strict scientific measurement|Government agencies operate purely as mathematical algorithms|Option A|Normative values deal with value judgments and what ought to be which complicates pure scientific objectivity in public administration.
3.1|Which of the following is considered a structural pillar when studying public administration through a scientific lens?|Spontaneous emotional responses|Arbitrary decision making|Span of control and hierarchy|Randomized political lobbying|Option C|Span of control and hierarchy are classic verifiable organizational principles studied when treating public administration as a science.
3.1|What is a central limitation of attempting to turn public administration into an exact physical science?|Public administration deals with living human societies rather than inanimate physical matter|Physical sciences do not use empirical observation unlike administration|Administration lacks any theoretical framework whatsoever|Human beings can be controlled in laboratories as easily as chemical elements|Option A|Public administration deals with complex human societies and behavior making it fundamentally different from predictable physical sciences.
3.1|How do the art and science perspectives interact within the study of public administration?|They contradict each other completely leaving no room for practical application|They complement one another by balancing empirical organizational structures with practical leadership skills|Science has completely replaced art in modern government operations|Art is considered entirely unscientific and irrelevant to public managers|Option B|Public administration requires both the empirical structural principles of science and the intuitive leadership skills of art to function effectively.

4.1|What primary objective is served by government economic regulation within the scope of public administration functions?|Preventing market failures, protecting consumer rights, and maintaining fair market competition|Eliminating all forms of private enterprise to establish total state-controlled production monopolies|Restricting international trade completely to protect domestic handicraft guilds|Ensuring absolute financial equality across every economic demographic without exception|Option A|Economic regulation is utilized by public administrators to correct market distortions, curb monopolies, and protect consumer interests.

3.1|How do proponents of Public Administration as a science justify their perspective?|Through the development of empirical observations and verifiable organizational principles like hierarchy|By arguing that human behavior can be completely predicted with 100 percent mathematical certainty|By proving that public policies are entirely free from cultural biases and political interference|Through the reliance on unverified leadership intuition over systematic data collection|Option A|Public Administration is viewed as a science by those who emphasize empirical observation, systematic study, and verifiable organizational principles such as hierarchy and span of control.
3.1|What was Robert Dahl's primary critique regarding the scientific status of Public Administration?|He argued it was too scientific and ignored the artistic qualities of human leadership|He claimed it could not be a pure science due to normative values, unpredictable human behavior, and cultural relativity|He stated that administrative principles were already universally valid across all cultures without exception|He believed that administrative theory was entirely dependent on biological evolution rather than social structures|Option B|Robert Dahl famously criticized Public Administration's claim to pure science by highlighting that administrative principles vary across cultures and are heavily influenced by normative values.
3.1|In the context of Study Session 3, why does unpredictable human behavior challenge Public Administration as a science?|Because human beings always obey bureaucratic rules without exception|Because science requires completely static, unchanging research subjects like laboratory chemicals|Because human actions and responses in organizations cannot always be anticipated or controlled under fixed laws|Because human behavior is exclusively driven by economic incentives rather than social motivations|Option C|Unpredictable human behavior poses a major challenge to scientific claims because people do not conform to standardized, unchanging laws in the way physical elements do.
3.1|What role do normative values play in Robert Dahl's evaluation of public administration principles?|They prove that administration is an exact physical science operating independently of human preference|They act as a barrier to creating value-free, universal scientific laws because what is considered good or desirable varies by society|They ensure that all administrative decisions are identical regardless of geographic location or cultural background|They are completely irrelevant to the study of organizational hierarchy and span of control|Option B|Normative values involve subjective ideas about what ought to be, making it impossible to establish universally neutral and objective scientific laws in public administration.
3.1|How does cultural relativity impact the concept of universal administrative principles according to Dahl?|It proves that a single organizational design works with equal effectiveness in every country on Earth|It suggests that administrative practices must be understood within the specific cultural and social context in which they operate|It demonstrates that culture has zero impact on how government employees execute public policies|It guarantees that leadership styles are identical across all global governments|Option B|Cultural relativity means administrative principles do not translate universally because different cultures shape organizational behavior and institutional expectations differently.
3.1|When a public administrator uses leadership skills to navigate a volatile social protest, which paradigm are they primarily exhibiting?|Public Administration as a pure physical science|Public Administration as an art|Public Administration as a strict mathematical equation|Public Administration as a closed laboratory experiment|Option B|Handling volatile social situations requires practical experience, intuition, and adaptive leadership, which align closely with Public Administration as an art.
3.1|Which of the following is considered a hallmark of viewing Public Administration through a scientific lens?|Relying solely on gut feeling during a crisis|Utilizing verifiable organizational principles such as span of control and formal hierarchy|Ignoring data collection in favor of artistic expression|Rejecting any systematic observation of bureaucratic structures|Option B|Verifiable organizational principles like span of control and hierarchy represent the structural, empirical focus of those who study administration as a science.
3.1|Why did Robert Dahl argue that the development of a science of public administration is hindered by environmental factors?|Because administrative institutions operate in dynamic political and social environments that constantly shift|Because government agencies never interact with the public or private sectors|Because administrative laws are written in stone and never change over time|Because environmental factors only affect private corporations and never public bureaucracies|Option A|Administrative systems are deeply embedded in shifting political, social, and cultural environments, making the formulation of static, universal scientific laws extremely difficult.
3.1|Which statement best summarizes the synthesis of art and science in modern Public Administration?|It is exclusively a hard science with no room for human judgment or creativity|It is purely an art form where systematic research and empirical data play zero role|It combines the structured, empirical observation of science with the practical intuition and leadership art required for real-world governance|It requires abandoning all organizational principles in favor of completely random decision-making|Option C|Effective public administration requires a balance of scientific organizational principles and the artistic, intuitive skills needed to manage complex human societies.

13.1|How did Scientific Management approach the selection and placement of personnel?|Through random assignment to promote flexibility|Through scientific selection and training based on capabilities|Through nepotism and personal recommendations|Through worker self-selection of job titles|Option B|Taylor emphasized scientific selection and training to ensure each worker's physical and mental capacities matched the specific demands of the job.

14.1|In Henri Fayol's framework of the 5 Elements of Administration what does the acronym POCCC stand for?|Planning Organizing Commanding Coordinating Controlling|Planning Operating Controlling Coordinating Commanding|Predicting Organizing Commanding Cooperating Centralizing|Planning Organizing Centralizing Communicating Controlling|Option A|POCCC stands for Planning Organizing Commanding Coordinating and Controlling representing the core managerial functions defined by Fayol.
14.1|Which of Henri Fayol's 14 principles specifically mandates that an employee should receive orders from only one superior to prevent conflicting instructions?|Unity of Direction|Scalar Chain|Unity of Command|Centralization|Option C|Unity of Command dictates that a worker should take orders from only one superior to avoid confusion and conflicting directives.
14.1|How does Fayol distinguish between Unity of Command and Unity of Direction?|Unity of direction focuses on a single boss while unity of command focuses on departmental budgeting|Unity of command means one superior per employee whereas unity of direction means one head and one plan for a group of activities having the same objective|Unity of command applies only to military organizations while unity of direction applies to private firms|There is no theoretical difference as Fayol used the terms interchangeably|Option B|Unity of command concerns dual subordination prevention while unity of direction ensures all activities with the same objective are aligned under one plan and head.
14.1|Which principle allows employees to bypass formal hierarchical channels in urgent situations provided their superiors are kept informed and approve?|Scalar Chain and the Gangplank|Centralization|Esprit de Corps|Span of Control|Option A|The gangplank allows horizontal communication across the scalar chain in emergency situations to speed up action while keeping managers informed.
14.1|What does Fayol's principle of Subordination of Individual Interest to General Interest mean?|The interests of an individual employee must always supersede organizational goals|Personal ambitions and departmental interests must yield to the overall goals and welfare of the entire organization|The government should control all private business interests|Employees are not permitted to have personal career goals|Option B|This principle ensures that the collective goals and interest of the organization take precedence over individual or sectional preferences.
14.1|Which administrative principle emphasizes the promotion of team spirit harmony and unity among organizational personnel?|Esprit de Corps|Initiative|Equity|Discipline|Option A|Esprit de Corps emphasizes building harmony and strong team spirit among personnel to foster organizational strength and cooperation.
14.1|According to Henri Fayol what is the exact definition of the principle of Initiative?|The power granted to a manager to hire and fire staff at will|The absolute right of top executives to make all strategic choices without consulting subordinates|The freedom for all employees to conceive and execute a plan at all levels of the organization demonstrating zeal and energy|The mandatory requirement for workers to arrive thirty minutes before their shifts start|Option C|Initiative empowers employees across the organization to think through and carry out plans creatively fostering active engagement and ownership.
14.1|Which of the following best describes Fayol's principle of Stability of Tenure of Personnel?|Employees should be rotated to a new department every three months to prevent boredom|Organization must provide lifetime employment guarantees regardless of economic performance|Frequent turnover of personnel is bad for organizational efficiency and sufficient time should be given for employees to settle into their roles|All workers must sign multi-year contracts before beginning their duties|Option C|Stability of tenure recognizes that high employee turnover is inefficient and that stability helps personnel master and successfully execute their duties.
14.1|In the context of Henri Fayol's 14 principles how are Authority and Responsibility related?|Responsibility is completely separate from authority and rests solely with the board of directors|Authority is the right to give orders and power to exact obedience while responsibility is the natural counterpart and accountability that comes with that authority|Authority applies only to informal groups while responsibility applies to legal contracts|Authority is a negative constraint whereas responsibility is an optional reward system|Option B|Fayol maintained that responsibility is the inevitable corollary of authority and wherever authority is exercised responsibility naturally arises.

12.1|Which of the following functions falls directly under the regulatory scope of statutory bodies?|Managing international diplomatic relations and signing global peace treaties|Oversighting specific industrial standards and ensuring compliance with public laws|Drafting national constitutions and adjudicating criminal court cases|Conducting private corporate mergers for multinational financial institutions|Option B|Regulatory boards and statutory bodies are empowered to oversee specific sectors, enforce industry standards, and ensure compliance with established legal frameworks.
12.1|What distinguishes privatization from commercialization in public sector reforms?|Privatization involves divesting government equity, whereas commercialization focuses on self-funding and profit-orientation while retaining state ownership|Privatization abolishes all corporate governance, whereas commercialization increases bureaucratic red tape|Privatization applies only to educational institutions, whereas commercialization applies exclusively to military defense|Privatization is managed by local traditional rulers, whereas commercialization is controlled by international courts|Option A|Privatization alters ownership by transferring government equity to private hands, whereas commercialization keeps ownership with the state while restructuring the enterprise to run on commercial principles.

15.1|Which core perspective of the Human Relations Theory fundamentally distinguishes it from classical management approaches?|Workers are viewed as Social Men motivated by belonging and group dynamics rather than mere financial incentives|Workers function best under strict hierarchical control and rigid standard operating procedures|Productivity is exclusively dictated by physical working conditions and economic optimization|Administrative efficiency relies solely on formal authority structures and clear chains of command|Option A|The Human Relations Theory shifted focus from purely economic and mechanical factors to the social and psychological needs of employees within organizations.
15.1|What was the primary finding observed during the Relay Assembly Test Room experiments within the Hawthorne Studies?|Worker output increased regardless of variations in rest periods and incentives due to the special attention they received|Production levels plummeted whenever lighting conditions were modified in any direction|Financial incentives were proven to be the single most effective driver of long-term output growth|Formal supervision was entirely unnecessary as long as automated assembly lines were operating efficiently|Option A|The Hawthorne Effect demonstrated that workers increased productivity simply because they felt valued and noticed as part of a special study group.
15.1|How did the Bank Wiring Observation Room phase of the Hawthorne Studies contribute to Public Administration thought?|It uncovered the powerful role of informal group norms and social pressures in regulating individual worker output|It proved that individual piece-rate financial incentives completely override group solidarity|It established that management could easily control informal cliques through strict disciplinary policies|It showed that physical fatigue was the primary determinant of employee performance and absenteeism|Option A|The Bank Wiring Room revealed that informal groups establish their own internal production ceilings and social norms, penalizing rate busters.
15.1|In the context of the Hawthorne Studies findings regarding the Bank Wiring Room, what did the term rate buster refer to?|An employee who produced too much work and violated informal group norms regarding acceptable output limits|A manager who illegally bypassed standard operating procedures to accelerate production schedules|A worker who consistently destroyed company equipment through reckless handling practices|A union representative who organized unauthorized strikes against management policies|Option A|A rate buster was a worker who exceeded the group-established production quota, threatening the informal social equilibrium.
15.1|What term is used in the Hawthorne Studies to describe workers who produced too little compared to the informal group standards?|Chiselers|Free riders|Agitators|Slackers|Option A|The Hawthorne studies identified chiselers as workers who produced below the informal group quota, alongside rate busters who produced too much.
15.1|Which intervention method was primarily utilized during the mass interviews phase of the Hawthorne research program?|Nondirective counseling allowing employees to freely express their feelings about work conditions and supervision|Strict quantitative questionnaires measuring physical fatigue against hourly wage rates|Controlled laboratory trials testing varying levels of chemical exposure and air quality|Open public town hall meetings presided over by high-ranking corporate executives|Option A|Mass interviews involved nondirective counseling techniques, giving workers a platform to voice their attitudes, grievances, and personal sentiments.
15.1|What was the initial focus of the illumination experiments conducted at the Hawthorne plant between 1924 and 1927?|To measure the direct relationship between physical lighting intensity and worker productivity|To evaluate the psychological impact of listening to classical music while assembling telephone relays|To assess the influence of participatory decision-making on employee morale and turnover rates|To test the effectiveness of decentralized management structures in manufacturing plants|Option A|The illumination experiments originally sought to determine if better or worse lighting physically altered worker output, leading to unexpected psychological discoveries.
15.1|Who is most famously associated as the principal pioneer and leading researcher behind the Hawthorne Studies at Western Electric?|Elton Mayo|Max Weber|Frederick Taylor|Woodrow Wilson|Option A|Elton Mayo and his associates led the landmark Hawthorne Studies, laying the foundational concepts for the Human Relations school of management.
15.1|Which concept best explains why employee behavior and output changed during the Hawthorne experiments simply because they knew they were being observed?|The Hawthorne Effect|The Peter Principle|Parkinson's Law|The Iron Law of Oligarchy|Option A|The Hawthorne Effect refers to the phenomenon where individuals modify their behavior in response to their awareness of being observed and studied.
15.1|What overarching conclusion regarding human behavior in organizations emerged from the cumulative findings of the Hawthorne Studies?|Organizational life is deeply social, requiring managers to account for informal relationships and human sentiment alongside formal structures|Organizations function most efficiently when human emotions are completely neutralized by strict rational rules|Financial compensation structures are the only reliable predictor of employee commitment and organizational loyalty|Formal organizational charts are entirely sufficient for predicting and controlling worker output in any setting|Option A|The Hawthorne Studies highlighted that organizations are social systems where informal dynamics, belonging, and recognition heavily influence worker behavior.
15.1|Which foundational research project marked the official beginning of the Human Relations Theory in Public Administration?|The Hawthorne Studies conducted between 1924 and 1932|The Taylor Time and Motion Studies on factory floors|The Weberian Bureaucratic Efficiency Trials of 1905|The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Evaluations|Option A|The Hawthorne Studies conducted at Western Electric laid the empirical groundwork for the Human Relations Theory by shifting focus to social factors.

13.1|What method did Taylor use to replace traditional rule-of-thumb practices in the workplace?|Intuitive managerial decision making|Systematic time-and-motion studies|Democratic employee voting|Seniority-based task allocation|Option B|Time-and-motion studies allowed managers to analyze every physical movement required for a task to determine the single most efficient way to perform it.

13.1|How did Scientific Management propose to handle the hiring and development of personnel?|Through random lottery assignments|Through scientific selection and training|Through hereditary succession models|Through unstructured peer recommendations|Option B|Scientific selection and training ensured that employees were explicitly matched to jobs matching their physical and mental capabilities and trained thoroughly to do them correctly.

13.1|Which financial incentive mechanism was heavily promoted under F.W. 13.1|What management structure replaced the traditional single-supervisor model under Taylor's functional foremanship?|A matrix management structure with temporary project leads|Multiple functional supervisors overseeing specialized aspects of a worker's tasks|A flat organizational hierarchy with no intermediate supervisors|A democratic workers council that elects daily operational leaders|Option B|Functional foremanship divided traditional supervisory responsibilities among multiple specialists, allowing workers to receive expert guidance in different areas of their job.
13.1|What was a primary criticism leveled against F.W. 2.1|Herbert Simon contributed to which conceptual framework of public administration by analyzing decision-making and administrative management?|The Integral View|The Holistic View|The Managerial View|The Mechanistic View|Option C|Herbert Simon is historically aligned with the administrative management school and the managerial view, which emphasizes upper-level direction, control, and decision-making structures.
2.1|How do Dimock and L.D. White collectively characterize the scope of public administration in the study session materials?|As a narrow set of executive actions|As an inclusive totality of all cooperative efforts toward goal attainment|As strictly limited to legal interpretations of statutes|As a purely technical mechanism for resource allocation|Option B|Dimock and L.D. White advocate for the integral view, defining public administration broadly as the total sum of all cooperative activities—clerical, manual, and managerial—required to realize goals.
2.2|According to Luther Gulick's administrative theory what does the acronym POSDCORB primarily represent?|The historical evolution of bureaucratic governance structures|The core functional phases and executive duties of public administration|The specific financial accounting procedures used in public agencies|The philosophical separation between politics and public administration|Option B|POSDCORB stands for Planning Organizing Staffing Directing Coordinating Reporting and Budgeting which outlines the executive functions of administration according to Luther Gulick.
2.2|Which specific component of POSDCORB involves establishing the formal structure of authority through which work is subdivided and coordinated?|Planning|Staffing|Organizing|Budgeting|Option C|Organizing involves setting up the formal structure of authority and dividing work subdivisions to ensure smooth organizational operations.
2.2|In the context of Luther Gulick's framework what does the 'D' in POSDCORB stand for?|Delegating|Directing|Designing|Developing|Option B|The acronym POSDCORB features two letters starting with D where the first represents Directing as a core executive function.
2.2|Which function within POSDCORB is primarily concerned with keeping those whom the executive is responsible informed through records research and inspection?|Reporting|Coordinating|Planning|Budgeting|Option A|Reporting ensures that the executive and superiors are kept informed of ongoing activities through records and inspection mechanisms.
2.2|What is the core argument of the Subject-Matter View against Luther Gulick's POSDCORB?|It focuses too heavily on specialized services rather than management techniques|It ignores the financial aspects of public agency management entirely|It reduces public administration to mere administrative techniques ignoring substantive public services|It places an excessive emphasis on democratic political accountability|Option C|The Subject-Matter View criticizes POSDCORB for treating administration purely as a set of generic techniques while ignoring substantive fields like health or education.
2.2|Which of the following falls under the critique raised by proponents of the Subject-Matter View of public administration?|Overlooking the importance of hierarchical coordination|Neglecting specialized functional services such as public health and national defense|Placing too much emphasis on budgeting and fiscal policy|Failing to account for the staffing needs of modern bureaucracies|Option B|The Subject-Matter View argues that administration must encompass specialized substantive public services like health education and defense rather than just administrative tools.
2.2|Which POSDCORB function entails working out in broad outline the things that need to be done and the methods for doing them to accomplish the enterprise purpose?|Planning|Organizing|Coordinating|Directing|Option A|Planning refers to the foundational executive task of outlining work objectives and the methods required to achieve them.
2.2|What does the 'B' in Luther Gulick's POSDCORB framework stand for?|Bureaucracy|Behavior|By-laws|Budgeting|Option D|Budgeting is the final letter in the POSDCORB acronym encompassing fiscal planning accounting and control.
2.2|Which executive function in POSDCORB involves the continuous inter-relation of the various parts of the work and the making of critical decisions?|Directing|Coordinating|Staffing|Reporting|Option B|Coordinating is the inter-relational function that binds different parts of an organization together to ensure harmonious work execution.
2.2|In the framework of POSDCORB what does the 'S' stand for?|Structuring|Supervising|Staffing|Strategy|Option C|Staffing refers to the personnel function of recruiting training and maintaining favorable conditions of work for staff.
3.1|Which characteristic primarily defines public administration when viewed as an art?|Strict adherence to universal mathematical models|Systematic laboratory experimentation with human behavior|Personal skill, intuition, and leadership in volatile situations|Standardized mechanical assembly line procedures|Option C|Viewing public administration as an art emphasizes personal skill, intuition, practical experience, and effective leadership in unpredictable social environments.
3.1|When public administration is analyzed through the lens of a science, what is its primary focus?|Empirical observation and verifiable organizational principles like hierarchy|Speculative philosophy and abstract moral theology|Completely random policy adjustments without structural foundations|Subjective emotional interpretation of individual artistic expression|Option A|Public administration as a science relies on empirical observation, systematic study, and the development of verifiable organizational principles such as hierarchy and span of control.
3.1|Which classical theorist is most famously associated with a rigorous critique questioning the scientific validity of public administration?|Max Weber|Robert Dahl|Woodrow Wilson|Luther Gulick|Option B|Robert Dahl famously critiqued the notion of public administration as a pure science due to normative values, human unpredictability, and cultural relativity.
3.1|According to Robert Dahl's critique, why is it difficult to establish universally valid administrative principles like in physical sciences?|Because administrative phenomena are entirely devoid of any human interaction|Because human behavior is unpredictable and administrative systems are culturally relative|Because computers are rarely utilized in public sector offices|Because historical archives are uniformly destroyed over time|Option B|Dahl argued that administration cannot be a pure science because human behavior varies unpredictably and administrative principles depend heavily on cultural contexts.
3.1|In the context of public administration, what role do normative values play according to Robert Dahl's critique?|They transform the discipline into an exact mathematical calculation|They invalidate the possibility of a value-free, pure science of administration|They ensure that every administrative decision is universally accepted worldwide|They eliminate the need for any formal organizational hierarchy|Option B|Normative values involve subjective ideas of what ought to be, which conflict with the objective detachment required by pure science and complicate universal claims.
3.1|Which organizational concept is typically examined when public administration is studied scientifically?|Emotional intuition and artistic flair|Span of control and structural hierarchy|Spontaneous poetic expression in policy documents|Creative fictional storytelling in bureaucratic reports|Option B|Hierarchy and span of control represent structural, verifiable organizational principles studied when public administration is treated as a science.
3.1|How does viewing public administration as an art differ from viewing it as a science?|Art relies on personal skill and practical experience while science relies on empirical observation and verifiable principles|Art focuses exclusively on computer coding while science focuses on painting murals|Art is universally identical across all cultures while science changes daily based on emotion|Art requires strict mathematical formulas while science requires random guesswork|Option A|The art perspective centers on practical experience and leadership skill, whereas the science perspective emphasizes empirical methods and structured principles.
3.1|Why did Robert Dahl state that administrative principles are culturally relative?|Because identical administrative structures produce identical cultural outcomes everywhere without exception|Because practices that work effectively in one society or culture may fail entirely in another|Because culture has no impact whatsoever on how government agencies function|Because all nations share the exact same historical background and administrative traditions|Option B|Cultural relativity means administrative effectiveness depends on specific societal values, traditions, and environments, preventing universal generalization.
3.1|What combination of attributes best describes the dual nature of public administration discussed in study session 3?|Purely mathematical and completely mechanical|Partially artistic through leadership and practical skill alongside scientific through empirical principles|Exclusively philosophical with zero practical applications|Strictly fictional and whimsical without real-world consequences|Option B|Public administration functions as both an art, requiring leadership and intuition, and a science, utilizing empirical observation and structural principles.
3.1|Which factor makes the study of public administration particularly challenging when attempting to make it a pure science?|The complete absence of any laws or regulations globally|The complexity and unpredictability of human behavior within social systems|The static and unchanging nature of all government institutions|The total lack of any historical records or case studies|Option B|Unpredictable human behavior creates variables that prevent public administration from achieving the absolute predictability found in natural sciences.

4.1|In the context of the functions of public administration, how is the maintenance of law and order traditionally categorized?|As a secondary auxiliary function unique to democratic regimes|As the foundational traditional function required to ensure societal stability and security|As an obsolete practice replaced entirely by modern welfare provisions|As an economic stabilization policy designed to curb inflation|Option B|The maintenance of law and order is the bedrock traditional function of any government, providing the secure framework necessary for citizens to live and commerce to operate safely.
4.1|Which function of public administration is primarily responsible for bridging traditional societal norms with contemporary developmental goals?|Economic regulation and taxation|Essential service delivery and infrastructure building|Social change and modernization|Military mobilization and border defense|Option C|Social change and modernization refer to the intentional public administration policies and programs designed to transform traditional behaviors, structures, and values to align with modern developmental objectives.
4.1|How do essential public services differ fundamentally under a modern welfare state compared to a historical laissez-faire state?|They are completely privatized and deregulated across all sectors|They are expanded comprehensively to cover cradle-to-grave needs such as healthcare, education, and social security|They are restricted exclusively to military personnel and high-ranking officials|They are funded entirely through voluntary charitable contributions rather than public taxation|Option B|Unlike the minimal state approach of the laissez-faire era, the modern welfare state proactively delivers a broad spectrum of essential cradle-to-grave services to guarantee baseline citizen well-being.
4.1|What foundational philosophy justified the minimal government intervention typical of the historical police state or laissez-faire era?|The belief that markets are inherently unstable and require constant state planning|The doctrine that government should primarily ensure security and property rights while leaving economic and social matters to private forces|The mandate that administration should control all means of production and distribution|The principle that social equality can only be achieved through total bureaucratic centralization|Option B|The laissez-faire philosophy argued for a night-watchman state where government involvement was strictly limited to defense, police protection, and enforcing contracts.
4.1|When a public agency implements universal healthcare programs and retirement pensions, which overarching phase of administrative evolution does it reflect?|The police state phase focused solely on criminal punishment|The transition toward a comprehensive cradle-to-grave welfare state|The isolationist foreign policy phase of public administration|The absolute monarchy model of public service delivery|Option B|Universal healthcare and pensions are hallmark programs of the modern welfare state, which expands public administration duties to safeguard citizens from cradle to grave.
4.1|Which administrative action best exemplifies the essential service delivery function of public administration?|Enacting legislation to outlaw corporate corruption|Deploying military troops to suppress an international border dispute|Operating municipal water treatment facilities and public transportation networks|Drafting long-term foreign trade agreements with allied nations|Option C|Essential service delivery encompasses the day-to-day operational responsibilities of public administration, such as providing clean water, power, sanitation, and transit to the populace.
4.1|Why did the traditional police state model eventually prove inadequate for rapidly industrializing societies?|Because industrialization eliminated the need for any form of central government|Because industrial societies generated complex socio-economic problems like poverty and labor exploitation that required active state intervention|Because citizens universally demanded the complete abolition of all legal codes|Because traditional police forces were too expensive to maintain during peacetime|Option B|The rise of industrialization created severe social inequalities and market failures that the hands-off police state could not address, forcing the evolution toward active public administration and welfare policies.
4.1|Which classification best describes public administration policies aimed at gender equality, literacy campaigns, and public health awareness?|Economic trade stabilization|Law and order enforcement|Social change and modernization|Laissez-faire deregulation|Option C|Literacy campaigns, public health initiatives, and equality policies are direct instruments of social change and modernization intended to uplift human capital and transform societal structures.
5.1|What core concept does the term administrative ecology primarily emphasize in the study of public administration?|The complete autonomy and isolation of bureaucratic structures from societal forces|The continuous interaction and mutual influence between administrative systems and their external environment|The absolute dominance of economic markets over governmental policy formulation|The historical evolution of legal frameworks governing civil service recruitment|Option B|Administrative ecology focuses on how public administration shapes and is shaped by its political, economic, and socio-cultural environment, a concept popularized by theorists like John Gaus and Fred Riggs.
5.1|Which scholar is most famously associated with introducing ecological principles and the environmental approach to public administration?|Max Weber|Woodrow Wilson|John Gaus|Luther Gulick|Option C|John Gaus pioneered the ecological approach to public administration, arguing that an agency's public policy and operations cannot be understood without examining its surrounding environmental setting.
5.1|Fred Riggs is best known in public administration literature for utilizing which conceptual framework to analyze administrative systems?|Prismatic and sala models within developing societies|Scientific management and time-and-motion studies|Ideal-type bureaucratic hierarchy and rational-legal authority|Classical POSDCORB managerial functions|Option A|Fred Riggs utilized the prismatic model and the concept of the sala to explain how administrative structures function differently in transitional or developing societies compared to fused or refracted societies.

5.1|According to the tenets of administrative ecology, what happens when an administrative system is transplanted from one cultural environment to another without adaptation?|It automatically achieves maximum efficiency and transparency|It often experiences dysfunction or friction because it fails to align with the host environment's political and social realities|It immediately transforms the host country into a fully modern industrial state|It ceases to exist due to a lack of legal documentation|Option B|Administrative ecology demonstrates that administrative systems are deeply embedded in their native environments; transplanting them without considering local ecological factors often leads to operational failure or mismatched expectations.

Taylor?|Rule-of-thumb methods|Charismatic leadership|Democratic participation|Decentralized decision-making|Option A|Taylor strongly advocated replacing traditional rule-of-thumb methods with systematic, scientific observation and experimentation.

13.1|What does F.W. 13.1|What is a primary criticism leveled against F.W. 14.1|How does Fayol distinguish Unity of Direction from Unity of Command?|Unity of direction refers to having one boss for each worker while unity of command refers to organizational goals|Unity of direction focuses on a single plan and head for activities sharing the same objective whereas unity of command focuses on a single direct supervisor|Unity of direction applies exclusively to financial accounting whereas unity of command applies to personnel management|Unity of direction is a lower-level supervisory tool whereas unity of command is strictly a board-level policy|Option B|Unity of direction ensures all related organizational activities are grouped under one plan and headed by one person to achieve a common objective, distinct from the single-boss rule of unity of command.

14.1|What is the core meaning of Esprit de Corps in the context of Fayol's administrative theory?|Strict hierarchical compliance among workers|Promoting team spirit harmony and organizational unity|Maximizing individual performance incentives|Centralizing operational authority at the executive level|Option B|Esprit de corps emphasizes building harmony team spirit and unity among organizational personnel to foster high morale and cooperation.
14.1|Under Fayol's administrative principles, what does the principle of subordination of individual interest mean?|Personal employee goals must always supersede corporate objectives|General organizational interests must take precedence over individual or sectional interests|Individual employees are prohibited from holding personal opinions at work|Departmental managers must ignore employee grievances to maintain discipline|Option B|This principle dictates that the interest of one employee or a group should not prevail over the goals and interests of the organization as a whole.
14.1|Which of the following best describes Fayol's principle of initiative?|The right of top executives to override standard operating procedures|The freedom for all personnel to propose and execute creative plans at various levels|The mandate that workers must independently design their own job descriptions|The obligation of managers to recruit new talent without human resource approval|Option B|Initiative involves empowering employees to conceive and carry out plans and ideas, which fosters deep engagement and organizational creativity.
14.1|Which principle addresses the fair, consistent, and equitable treatment of all subordinates by managers combining kindliness and justice?|Discipline|Equity|Remuneration|Stability of tenure|Option B|Equity combines kindliness and justice among managers to ensure fair treatment and loyalty from the workforce.
14.1|Why did Fayol advocate for stability of tenure of personnel as a core administrative principle?|To minimize the heavy costs and productivity losses associated with frequent employee turnover|To ensure that workers never seek promotions into higher management tiers|To prevent employees from forming informal social groups in the workplace|To guarantee that salaries remain fixed indefinitely without annual adjustments|Option A|Stability of tenure recognizes that frequent turnover is inefficient and that time is required for employees to learn and successfully execute their organizational roles.
