12.1|Why might a poorly managed public corporation become a financial burden to the government?|Because it relies heavily on government subventions and bailouts due to inefficiency|Because commercial enterprises never generate any operational revenue under state control|Because statutory bodies are legally barred from charging fees for public utilities|Because private shareholders demand immediate dividend payouts from public funds|Option A|Inefficient public corporations often require continuous financial support and subventions from the national treasury, turning them into economic drains.
12.1|What is a key governance challenge often addressed by public enterprise reforms like privatization?|Excessive political interference and bureaucratic inefficiency in commercial operations|The complete absence of government regulations across all private industrial sectors|An overwhelming surplus of skilled private sector management personnel in civil service|The immediate elimination of consumer demand for public utility services|Option A|Privatization and commercialization aim to remove public enterprises from stifling political interference and bureaucratic bottlenecks, enhancing operational efficiency.
13.1|Who is widely recognized as the father of Scientific Management Theory within public administration and management history|Max Weber|Woodrow Wilson|Frederick Winslow Taylor|Henri Fayol|Option C|F.W. Taylor is globally acknowledged as the father of Scientific Management for pioneering systematic approaches to workplace efficiency.
13.1|What core workplace phenomenon did Frederick Taylor seek to eliminate through time-and-motion studies and systematic management|Bureaucratic red tape|Worker soldiering|Executive corruption|Groupthink dynamics|Option B|Worker soldiering refers to workers deliberately restricting their output, which Taylor aimed to eradicate using scientific measurement.
13.1|What fundamental replacement did Scientific Management propose in place of traditional workplace estimation|Rule-of-thumb methods with empirical science|Political patronage with civil service merit|Centralized planning with decentralized autonomy|Informal social norms with rigid legal statutes|Option A|Taylor famously advocated for replacing inefficient rule-of-thumb methods with scientifically analyzed data and standard procedures.
13.1|Which of the following best describes the core principle known as the mental revolution in Taylorism|A psychological counseling program for stressed employees|A cooperative shift in focus from dividing the surplus to increasing total output|A legal mandate replacing private ownership with state control|A transition from manual labor to automated robotics|Option B|The mental revolution requires both management and workers to stop fighting over the surplus and instead cooperate to expand it.
13.1|Which mechanism was utilized under Scientific Management to determine the absolute one best way to perform a physical task|Psychometric intelligence testing|Time-and-motion studies|Participatory action research|Longitudinal ethnographic observation|Option B|Time-and-motion studies break tasks down into elemental movements to eliminate wasted motion and identify the most efficient method.
13.1|How did Scientific Management theory fundamentally approach worker selection and development|Through random job assignment and peer training|Through hereditary succession and apprenticeship|Through scientific selection matched with specialized training|Through self-directed task rotation across departments|Option C|Taylor stressed that workers should be scientifically selected for specific roles and trained systematically rather than assigned arbitrarily.
13.1|What was the primary purpose of introducing the piece-rate wage system in Taylor's framework|To encourage workers to maximize output by linking pay directly to individual productivity|To ensure absolute income equality among all factory floor employees|To guarantee a fixed annual salary regardless of output fluctuations|To penalize employees who took unauthorized coffee breaks|Option A|The piece-rate system financially incentivized high productivity by paying workers strictly based on the number of units they produced.
13.1|What organizational arrangement did functional foremanship introduce to the traditional single-supervisor model|Replacing all supervisors with automated artificial intelligence algorithms|Assigning multiple specialized functional bosses to oversee different aspects of a worker's duties|Rotating the managerial role among line workers on a weekly basis|Eliminating all middle management to flatten the organizational hierarchy completely|Option B|Functional foremanship broke supervision into distinct specialized areas, allowing multiple expert foremen to oversee different dimensions of a worker's job.
13.1|What was a primary and persistent criticism leveled against Taylor's Scientific Management Theory|It fostered excessive bureaucracy that slowed down emergency response times|It treated workers merely as mechanical parts and an economic man focused solely on monetary gain|It relied too heavily on subjective intuition rather than hard quantitative metrics|It granted excessive democratic power to low-level assembly line operatives|Option B|Critics frequently condemned Taylorism for reducing complex human laborers to mere extensions of machines driven purely by financial motives.
13.1|Under Taylor's principles of Scientific Management, how was administrative and operational responsibility distributed|Concentrated entirely among the factory floor workers to promote self-management|Transferred fully to labor unions to ensure fair industrial democracy|Divided clearly between management who plan and workers who execute tasks|Assigned randomly to committees to foster collaborative consensus|Option C|Taylor advocated for a strict division of responsibility where managers assume the planning role and workers focus solely on execution.
14.1|Which administrative theorist is best known for developing a top-management perspective that outlines five primary elements of management and fourteen administrative principles?|Max Weber|Henri Fayol|Frederick Winslow Taylor|Woodrow Wilson|Option B|Henri Fayol introduced the top-management perspective encompassing the five elements of management (POCCC) and fourteen administrative principles.
14.1|In Henri Fayol's POCCC framework, which element of management involves ensuring that all activities of an organization are synchronized and that efforts are harmonized toward a common goal?|Planning|Organizing|Commanding|Coordinating|Option D|Coordinating focuses on unifying, harmonizing, and synchronizing all organizational activities and efforts to ensure smooth operations.
14.1|Which of Henri Fayol's fourteen principles emphasizes that an employee should receive orders from one superior only to prevent dual command conflicts?|Unity of Direction|Unity of Command|Scalar Chain|Centralization|Option B|Unity of Command dictates that an employee should take orders from only one direct supervisor to avoid conflicting instructions and confusion.
14.1|What does Henri Fayol's principle of Scalar Chain traditionally refer to within an organizational hierarchy?|The formal line of authority reaching from top management to the lowest ranks|The concentration of decision-making authority at the executive level|The equitable distribution of financial rewards and remuneration|The promotion of team spirit and harmony among personnel|Option A|The scalar chain represents the unbroken chain of hierarchical authority and communication running from the highest executive to the lowest operative.
14.1|What mechanism did Henri Fayol introduce to allow direct lateral communication between employees at the same hierarchical level while bypassing the strict scalar chain in emergencies?|The Gangplank|The Centralized Hub|The Unity Link|The Command Bridge|Option A|The gangplank allows peers across different departments to communicate directly with management approval, bypassing lengthy scalar chain delays.
14.1|According to Henri Fayol's fourteen principles, which concept requires that the general interest of the organization must take precedence over the personal interests of individual employees?|Subordination of individual interest to the general interest|Esprit de Corps|Initiative|Stability of tenure of personnel|Option A|This principle mandates that organizational goals must always supersede personal or sectional interests for the collective good of the enterprise.
14.1|Which of the five elements in Fayol's POCCC model is primarily focused on examining the future and charting a course of action through a comprehensive blueprint?|Planning|Organizing|Commanding|Controlling|Option A|Planning involves looking ahead, assessing future conditions, and formulating a course of action to achieve organizational objectives effectively.
14.1|What does Henri Fayol's principle of Esprit de Corps seek to foster within a public or private organization?|Strict obedience to bureaucratic rules and regulations|A sense of team spirit, harmony, and unity among personnel|The reduction of unnecessary operational expenditures|The centralization of authority at the topmost management level|Option B|Esprit de Corps emphasizes building morale, harmony, and cooperative team spirit among workers to strengthen organizational solidarity.
14.1|Which administrative principle by Henri Fayol addresses the reduction of employee turnover by providing job security and career stability?|Remuneration|Equity|Stability of tenure of personnel|Discipline|Option C|Stability of tenure ensures that employees have job security and adequate time to settle into their roles, minimizing costly turnover.
14.1|In the context of Henri Fayol's fourteen principles, what does the principle of Equity combine to guide managerial behavior toward subordinates?|Strict discipline and absolute centralized authority|Fairness combined with kindness and justice in treating employees|High financial remuneration and competitive bonuses|Clear division of labor and specialized task assignments|Option B|Equity combines kindliness and justice on the part of managers to ensure subordinates are treated fairly and loyally.
15.1|Which core perspective of the Human Relations Theory challenges the classical economic view of workers?|Workers are viewed strictly as rational economic beings seeking maximum wages|Workers are treated as social men motivated by belonging recognition and group dynamics|Workers are primarily driven by rigid hierarchical control and formal authority structures|Workers act entirely independently without influence from peer groups or management|Option B|The Human Relations Theory redefines the worker from a purely economic actor to a social man driven by psychological and social needs.
15.1|What was the primary finding of the illumination experiments conducted during the early phase of the Hawthorne Studies?|Physical lighting levels had a direct and linear correlation with worker productivity|Wage incentives completely overshadowed the physical environment in determining output|Productivity increased or remained high even when lighting conditions varied because workers responded to attention|Natural lighting proved vastly superior to artificial illumination in every industrial test setting|Option C|The illumination experiments revealed that output increased regardless of lighting adjustments due to the psychological impact of being observed.
15.1|What phenomenon was discovered in the Relay Assembly Room experiments where output rose due to special attention?|The Hawthorne Effect|The Peter Principle|The Iron Law of Oligarchy|The Scalar Chain|Option A|The Hawthorne Effect describes the phenomenon where individuals modify their behavior in response to their awareness of being observed.
15.1|How did the mass interview program change the focus of the Hawthorne research team?|It confirmed that technical supervision was the single most important determinant of morale|It shifted the emphasis from purely physical working conditions to worker attitudes grievances and social dynamics|It proved that financial grievances were the root cause of all industrial conflict|It demonstrated that individual interviews were ineffective compared to large group surveys|Option B|The mass interviews redirected attention away from physical variables toward employee perceptions interpersonal relations and workplace grievances.
15.1|What distinct behavioral pattern was uncovered during the Bank Wiring Room observation phase?|Workers competed fiercely against one another to maximize daily piece-rate earnings|Informal group norms emerged to restrict output and penalize rate busters and chiselers|Management successfully enforced strict production quotas through peer pressure|Employees abandoned all informal structures in favor of formal organizational rules|Option C|The Bank Wiring Room revealed that informal work groups established internal production ceilings and socially penalized peers who exceeded or fell below them.
15.1|Who is recognized as the principal founding theorist and leader behind the Hawthorne Studies at Western Electric?|Frederick Winslow Taylor|Max Weber|Elton Mayo|Chester Barnard|Option C|Elton Mayo led the research team at the Hawthorne Works, laying the empirical foundations for the Human Relations school of management.
15.1|According to the Human Relations Theory what primary factor influences worker satisfaction and productivity?|Strict adherence to standard operating procedures and bureaucratic rules|The presence of fear and strict managerial oversight|Inclusion in informal social groups and recognition of human needs|Maximization of piece-rate financial incentives above all else|Option C|Social recognition, group belonging, and satisfying interpersonal dynamics are core drivers of worker satisfaction and productivity under this theory.
15.1|In the context of the Hawthorne Studies what does the term rate buster refer to?|A worker who produces significantly more than the informal group quota and breaks group norms|A machine operator who consistently sabotages equipment to protest low wages|An efficiency expert who implements scientific management techniques|A supervisor who imposes unfair production standards on the factory floor|Option A|A rate buster is a worker who violates informal group norms by producing output above the socially accepted ceiling.
15.1|Which of the following best describes a chiseler in the dynamics of the Bank Wiring Room?|A worker who steals tools from the company inventory|A worker who produces significantly less than the informal group standard|A manager who reduces wages arbitrarily during production peaks|An employee who acts as a liaison between union representatives and management|Option B|A chiseler is an informal term used by work groups to describe someone who produces below the established group norm.
15.1|What was a major theoretical shift brought about by the transition from Classical Theory to Human Relations Theory?|From viewing organizations as open social systems to closed mechanical systems|From focusing exclusively on formal structures and economic incentives to recognizing informal organization and social needs|From prioritizing psychological factors to completely ignoring human emotions in the workplace|From emphasizing democratic leadership to enforcing strict military-style command chains|Option B|The Human Relations Theory expanded administrative thought by integrating informal organizations and psychological needs into the study of management.

14.1|How does Fayol distinguish between Unity of Command and Unity of Direction?|Unity of command concerns one boss per employee while unity of direction concerns one head and one plan for a group of activities having the same objective|Unity of command refers to departmental budgeting while unity of direction refers to hierarchical scalar chains|Unity of command focuses on discipline while unity of direction focuses on equitable remuneration|Unity of command relates to top-management while unity of direction relates to lower-level workers|Option A|Unity of Command ensures single-superior reporting lines, whereas Unity of Direction unifies efforts toward a single shared plan or objective for activities with the same goal.

14.1|According to Fayol, what does the principle of subordination of individual interest mean?|Personal interests must be secondary to the general interest of the organization|Employees must prioritize individual career progression over group goals|Departmental interests should override overall corporate objectives|Management interests must always supersede employee remuneration|Option A|This principle dictates that the interest of an individual employee or group must not take precedence over the goals and interests of the organization as a whole.

13.1|Which core principle of Scientific Management involves both management and workers shifting their focus from dividing the surplus to increasing company output?|Mental revolution cooperation|Division of responsibility|Scientific selection and training|Functional foremanship|Option A|The mental revolution requires management and labor to stop fighting over the division of profits and instead cooperate to expand total output, benefiting both parties.|

13.1|Which compensation structure was heavily promoted by Taylor to incentivize high productivity among industrial workers?|Profit-sharing schemes across the entire enterprise|Fixed annual salaries regardless of output levels|Piece-rate wage system tied directly to units produced|Seniority-based incremental raises over time|Option C|The piece-rate wage system rewarded workers financially based on the exact number of units they produced, aligning personal earnings with output goals.|
13.1|What was a major and recurring criticism leveled against Taylor's Scientific Management Theory regarding human workers?|It treated workers as passive machine parts or economic men|It was overly focused on emotional intelligence at the expense of output|It decentralized authority to an unsustainable degree|It relied too heavily on employee self-management and autonomy|Option A|Critics frequently condemned scientific management for viewing workers merely as economic men and extensions of factory machinery rather than complex social beings.|
13.1|Under the division of responsibility principle in scientific management, what was assigned as the primary duty of management?|Performing all physical labor alongside the shop floor employees|Gathering traditional knowledge and transforming it into scientific laws|Establishing democratic cooperatives with equal voting shares|Handling external public relations and government compliance exclusively|Option B|Management was tasked with gathering traditional, unstructured knowledge from workers, analyzing it scientifically, and developing standardized rules and procedures.|

8.1|What is the primary distinguishing motive between public administration and private administration according to administrative theory?|Public administration seeks profit generation while private administration focuses on universal welfare|Public administration aims at public service and community welfare whereas private administration is driven by profit maximization|Public administration operates entirely on voluntary contributions while private administration relies on state subsidies|Public administration prioritizes individual shareholder returns while private administration answers directly to voters|Option B|Public administration is fundamentally driven by the motive of public service and social welfare, whereas private administration prioritizes generating profit for its owners or shareholders.
8.1|How do public and private organizations typically differ in their primary sources of revenue generation?|Public organizations rely primarily on tax revenues and public funds while private organizations generate revenue through the sale of goods and services|Public organizations depend on venture capital while private organizations rely on government grants|Public organizations generate income exclusively through user fees while private organizations are funded by mandatory levies|Public organizations rely on corporate stock offerings while private organizations depend on philanthropic donations|Option A|Public administration is financed largely through compulsory taxes, fees, and public appropriations, whereas private administration relies on voluntary market transactions, sales, and investments.
8.1|From an accountability perspective, to whom is public administration ultimately answerable in a democratic system?|To private equity holders and board members elected by institutional investors|To the general public, courts, legislatures, and elected political representatives|To market competitors and industry standard-setting trade associations|To internal corporate auditors and private auditing firms hired by executives|Option B|Public administration operates under public scrutiny and is legally and politically accountable to citizens, the courts, and legislative oversight bodies, unlike private entities which answer primarily to shareholders.
8.1|Which traditional theorists are most closely associated with advocating the strict Politics-Administration Dichotomy?|Paul Appleby and Dwight Waldo|Max Weber and Henri Fayol|Woodrow Wilson and Frank Goodnow|Herbert Simon and Chester Barnard|Option C|Woodrow Wilson and Frank Goodnow were early pioneers who argued for a strict conceptual and structural separation between politics and administration.
8.1|What was the core argument advanced by Woodrow Wilson and Frank Goodnow regarding the relationship between politics and administration?|Administration should actively dictate legislative agendas while politicians execute them|Politics formulates policy and makes value choices while administration is a neutral instrument focused on efficient execution|Politics and administration are identical functions that cannot be separated in any bureaucratic structure|Administration creates public laws while politicians manage day-to-day government agency operations|Option B|The classical dichotomy posits that politics is concerned with policy formulation and political will, whereas administration is a distinct, value-neutral sphere focused on efficient implementation.
8.1|Which scholars strongly challenged the classical Politics-Administration Dichotomy by arguing that administrators are deeply involved in policy formulation?|Woodrow Wilson and Frank Goodnow|Paul Appleby and Dwight Waldo|Frederick Taylor and Luther Gulick|Max Weber and Robert Michels|Option B|Paul Appleby and Dwight Waldo argued against the dichotomy, demonstrating that public administrators exercise discretion and play a vital, active role in shaping public policy.
8.1|Why do critics of the classical Politics-Administration Dichotomy assert that administrative agencies cannot remain entirely neutral?|Because bureaucrats are legally prohibited from voting or participating in public elections|Because administrative decision-making inherently involves discretionary choices, resource allocation, and value judgments that influence policy outcomes|Because public agencies are funded entirely by private market revenues rather than legislative appropriations|Because administrators are elected directly by citizens to draft new constitutional amendments|Option B|Administrative agencies exercise substantial discretion when translating broad laws into concrete rules, making them active participants in policy formulation rather than purely mechanical executors.
8.1|In terms of structural environment and operational constraints, how do public and private organizations generally compare?|Public organizations operate in a highly transparent, legally constrained political environment whereas private organizations operate with greater internal autonomy and market flexibility|Public organizations enjoy complete freedom from legislative oversight while private organizations are heavily regulated by municipal courts|Public organizations prioritize market competitiveness over legal compliance whereas private organizations are bound by constitutional due process|Public organizations focus exclusively on cost-reduction strategies while private organizations focus solely on equity and fairness|Option A|Public administration must adhere strictly to constitutional guidelines, transparency laws, and political accountability, giving it less operational flexibility than private enterprises operating in market environments.
8.1|Which financial characteristic distinguishes public revenue collection from private revenue models?|Public revenue is entirely voluntary through subscription fees while private revenue is compulsory|Public revenue relies on mandatory assessments like taxes backed by legal authority while private revenue depends on voluntary customer purchases|Public revenue is generated strictly through international stock markets while private revenue comes from municipal bonds|Public revenue is derived exclusively from corporate dividends while private revenue comes from tariffs|Option B|Public administration utilizes the coercive and legal authority of the state to collect taxes and fees, distinguishing it from private organizations that rely on voluntary exchange in the market.
8.1|How does the evaluation of success or performance differ fundamentally between public and private administration?|Public success is measured by profit margins while private success is measured by social equity and democratic responsiveness|Public success is gauged by public satisfaction, statutory compliance, and service delivery while private success is evaluated primarily through profitability and financial viability|Public success is determined by private shareholder dividends while private success is determined by legislative approval ratings|Public success is assessed by market share competition while private success is assessed by judicial review outcomes|Option B|Because their driving motives differ, public administration evaluates performance based on public service delivery, legal adherence, and social impact, whereas private administration measures success through profit and financial return.

9.1|How are standard procedures typically implemented within a formal organization|Through impulsive, verbal agreements between peers|Via impersonal, documented rules and standard guidelines|Through unwritten social codes and cultural habits|Via spontaneous emotional adjustments by workers|Option B|Formal organizations rely on impersonal standard procedures that are documented and applied uniformly rather than arbitrarily.

9.1|Why might an administrator study the informal organization within a public bureaucracy|To rewrite the official structural charts every week|To understand how grapevines and social networks influence morale and communication|To eliminate all personal interaction among workers permanently|To ensure that standard operating procedures are ignored entirely|Option B|Understanding the informal organization helps managers recognize how communication grapevines and social networks impact overall organizational performance.
9.1|What distinguishes the communication channels of a formal organization from those of an informal one|Formal channels rely on official charts while informal ones rely on grapevines|Formal channels use unwritten norms while informal ones use strict laws|Formal channels are entirely emotional while informal ones are purely structural|Formal channels are unpredictable while informal ones follow rigid public schedules|Option A|Formal communication follows prescribed hierarchical channels and charts, whereas informal communication relies on organic networks like grapevines.
9.1|What is a likely consequence if management attempts to completely eradicate the informal organization in a workplace|Increased alignment with impersonal standard procedures|Improved efficiency across all hierarchical levels|Employee resistance and disruption of morale as psychological needs go unmet|A seamless transition to a purely rational-legal bureaucracy|Option C|Attempting to suppress informal social structures usually triggers resistance because it deprives workers of the peer connections that fulfill vital psychological needs.
